title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 1: An Extraordinary Court
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's December 28, 2008 Inquirer column explaining why the Philippine Supreme Court is 'extraordinary,' wielding more powers and duties than any comparable tribunal, even the United States'

The Court's two constitutional judicial DUTIES -- to settle actual controversies and to determine 'grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction' by any branch -- the second being an extraordinary, 'activist'/'interventionist' check born of the martial-law experience and unknown to most foreign courts

Its 'quasi-legislative' work (promulgating court rules, running the bar, regulating the practice of law, the IBP and MCLE, and the writs of amparo and habeas data) and its 'quasi-executive' work (administrative supervision over 2,000+ judges and 26,000 personnel)

The civic point that, being given so much, the Court is expected to use these exceptional powers solely for the people, as 'the last bulwark of democracy and the impregnable citadel of liberty' -- 'to whom much is given, much is expected'
sub_topics: The Court's recent extraordinary feats: stopping the 1997 and 2006 people's-initiative Charter revisions, defrocking Estrada and validating Arroyo's ascent in 2001, annulling PP 1017, and nullifying acts of Congress and government contracts

Why the 1987 Constitution armed the judiciary: the martial-law experience under Marcos prompted a grant of both 'ordinary and extraordinary authority to check the abuses and excesses of the other branches'

Duties, not mere powers: the Constitution speaks of 'duties' -- a power may be relinquished but a duty 'cannot under any circumstance be evaded'; the Court 'cannot shirk, waver or equivocate,' on pain of being censured for dereliction
Unelected checking the elected: the Court's 'democratic constituency is the Constitution,' overwhelmingly ratified by the people, so its loyalty is to the Charter, not the President or Congress

Ordinary vs. extraordinary jurisdiction: reviewing lower courts and agencies is the 'ordinary' duty most supreme courts share; striking down 'gravely abusive' acts of government is the extraordinary function -- no foreign court (unlike Thailand's constitutional court or Russia's administrative court) dispenses 'grave abuse' judgments, yet ours holds sole jurisdiction over all of them

Quasi-legislative functions: enacting rules of procedure, conducting the bar exams, regulating and disciplining lawyers, requiring IBP membership and triennial MCLE, and issuing the rules on the writ of amparo (Sept. 25, 2007) and the writ of habeas data

Quasi-executive functions: 'administrative supervision over all courts and the personnel thereof' -- appointing a court administrator to oversee 2,000+ judges and 26,000 personnel, disciplining staff, assigning judges, and handling courthouses and supplies; once appointed, judges relate to the Court alone, not the Executive

stances.claim: The 1987 Constitution deliberately gave the judiciary 'extraordinary' authority -- chiefly the duty to strike down 'grave abuse of discretion' by any branch -- precisely because of the martial-law experience, making ours a more powerful court than even the US Supreme Court.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-justification: rooting the Court's exceptional power in the trauma of dictatorship to explain why it is intentionally 'activist'

stances.claim: These are DUTIES, not mere powers -- 'a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot... be evaded' -- so the Court 'cannot shirk, waver or equivocate,' and its loyalty runs to the Constitution (its true democratic constituency), not to the President or Congress.
stances.rhetorical_move: duty-vs-power distinction: converting the Court's authority into an inescapable obligation to act against abuse

stances.claim: Because the Court holds judicial, quasi-legislative and quasi-executive powers greater than any comparable tribunal, it must use them 'solely for [the people's] benefit' as 'the last bulwark of democracy and the impregnable citadel of liberty' -- 'to whom much is given, much is expected.'
stances.rhetorical_move: stewardship close: pairing the catalogue of powers with a moral expectation of fidelity to the public

notable_anecdotes: The diplomats' amazement: CJP opens with friends 'especially in the diplomatic corps' marveling at the Court's outsized role in recent Philippine history -- halting Charter revisions, unseating a president, voiding proclamations and contracts.

No foreign 'grave abuse' court: he notes that while some countries split the work among supreme, constitutional (Thailand) and administrative (Russia) courts, he knows of no foreign tribunal that renders 'grave abuse' judgments -- a power unique to ours.

The MCLE leash: he cites how the Court not only runs the bar but requires lawyers to take continuing legal education every three years 'or they would lose their licenses' -- an illustration of its quasi-legislative reach.
2,000 judges, 26,000 staff: he quantifies the Court's quasi-executive burden, supervising the entire judicial workforce through a court administrator, to show the scale of its administrative duty.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's December 28, 2008 Inquirer column, explains why the Philippine Supreme Court is 'extraordinary' -- wielding, he argues, more powers and duties than any comparable tribunal, even the United States'. He opens with the diplomats' amazement at the Court's recent feats: halting the 1997 and 2006 people's-initiative Charter revisions, defrocking Estrada and validating Arroyo's ascent in 2001, annulling PP 1017, and voiding acts of Congress and government contracts. The 1987 Constitution armed the judiciary this way, he says, because of the martial-law experience, imposing two judicial DUTIES: to settle actual controversies and to determine 'grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction' by any branch. He stresses that these are duties, not mere powers -- 'a power can be relinquished but a duty cannot... be evaded' -- so the Court 'cannot shirk, waver or equivocate,' and is in this sense mandated to be 'activist' and 'interventionist'; its 'democratic constituency is the Constitution,' so its loyalty runs to the Charter, not the President or Congress. The first duty (reviewing lower courts) is the 'ordinary' one most supreme courts share; the second (striking down grave abuse) is extraordinary and, he notes, unknown to foreign courts that split such work among constitutional (Thailand) and administrative (Russia) tribunals. Beyond judging, the Court holds 'quasi-legislative' power (promulgating court rules, running the bar, regulating lawyers, the IBP and triennial MCLE, and issuing the writs of amparo and habeas data) and 'quasi-executive' power ('administrative supervision over all courts,' overseeing 2,000-plus judges and 26,000 personnel through a court administrator). Endowed with more than any comparable tribunal, he concludes, the Court is expected to use these powers solely for the people, as 'the last bulwark of democracy and the impregnable citadel of liberty' -- 'to whom much is given, much is expected.'
